summary: Identifies protocols and applications that break when a NAT sits in the path, and notes known workarounds. It is not exhaustive. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: NAT can change a packet's address while leaving addresses written inside the application data unchanged. RFC 3027 surveys protocols that can be affected and describes some workarounds.

questions: what is an alg in nat
why does ftp not work through nat
which protocols have problems with nat
subtitle: Examples of Internet protocols that can fail when address translation sits between endpoints.

tldr.problem: NAT changes addresses in packet headers, while some applications put addresses or ports in their data or depend on connections initiated from either direction.
tldr.mechanism: The memo groups common causes of failure and surveys protocols that cannot work through NAT, protocols that may need an Application Level Gateway, and an application designed to work with NAT.
tldr.outcome: It is a non-comprehensive Informational survey of problems and known workarounds, not an endorsement of NAT.

today: RFC 3027 is Informational. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Survey Covers
sections.content:
NAT changes endpoint addresses in IP headers and keeps state so traffic can be routed between address realms. An application-specific Application Level Gateway (ALG) may also inspect and rewrite the packet payload.

RFC 3027 lists protocols and applications known to have problems when NAT is in the path. The authors state that the list is incomplete and that the document is intended to identify complications, not to advocate NAT.
sections.plainLanguage: NAT changes packet headers. Some applications also put addresses in their messages, so a helper may need to understand and change the application data too.

sections.title: Common Reasons Protocols Break
sections.content:
The memo identifies several patterns: realm-specific addresses in payloads; a control connection that opens separate data connections; peer-to-peer traffic that can start from either side; IP fragmentation with NAPT; applications that need an address mapping retained across sessions; and applications that need more public addresses than are available.

An ALG may help with unencrypted payloads, but secured data may prevent the gateway from reading or changing the embedded information. NAT also cannot infer that separate connections belong to one application session unless it understands that protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Problems arise when a program writes network addresses inside its message, opens a second connection, or needs the other side to start a connection back.

sections.title: Protocols That Resist Translation
sections.content:
The memo says end-to-end IPsec is severely hampered by NAT. Authentication Header detects changes to IP headers, and encrypted Encapsulating Security Payload can hide the transport header fields NAT would need to update. IKE may also carry protected IP addresses.

Kerberos tickets are encrypted and can contain the address for which they are valid, so an ALG cannot simply rewrite them. The memo also describes X Window System and RSH issues where addresses or ports appear in protocol data or connections are initiated in the reverse direction.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption and integrity checks can stop an intermediary from changing an address. Some protocols also reveal a private address or expect a connection to start from outside.

sections.title: Examples Where an ALG May Help
sections.content:
FTP includes data-port information in its control commands, so an FTP ALG must inspect both PORT and PASV exchanges and update packet lengths, checksums and sequence numbers. DNS may need a DNS-ALG to translate addresses in questions and answers; DNSSEC protection prevents such editing.

The memo also discusses RSVP, SMTP, SIP, RealAudio, H.323 and SNMP. Each has specific constraints, such as addresses in payloads, dynamically chosen ports, security protection or multiple related connections. Some can use an ALG or proxy; none is described as having a universal workaround.
sections.plainLanguage: An ALG can help only when it understands the protocol and can safely edit its messages. Encryption, changing packet sizes and multiple connections make that work harder.

sections.title: An Application Designed for NAT
sections.content:
The memo describes the proprietary Activision Games protocol as designed to work through NAT without an ALG. A player contacts a global address server, which learns private address information from the message and external address information from packet headers.

The server shares both addresses with other players, which try direct connections using whichever address works. The approach depends on NAT retaining the same mapping during the game session; NAPT must also allow multiple simultaneous UDP connections using the assigned address and port.
sections.plainLanguage: The game server tells players both the private and external addresses for each peer. Players try a direct connection, while NAT must keep the address mapping available during the session.
